title: A case study structure clients can approve
metaTitle: Approve the case study before art
excerpt: Show a case-study draft early, and agree what may be public: the name, the numbers, and the screens. A study that surprises the client does not get published.
alt: A white modernist building with stacked cubic volumes and tall windows against a pale sky. A structure you can read from the outside, the way a case study should read.
caption: Volumes you can tell apart before you go in. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a client see a case study?
faqs.answer: Show an outline first: a headline, a few sentences, and the list of screens. Ask whether it is true and whether you may say it, before anyone designs the page. A polished layout is the wrong moment for the first look, because changing a sentence then feels like rejecting a finished object.

faqs.question: What needs an explicit yes?
faqs.answer: The name, the screens, any number, and any quote. If you do not have permission and a real source, leave the number out. A quote has to be a sentence they said and approved, not a polished line they would not speak. Save the written approval, and do not add new facts after it.

faqs.question: What if they need the study taken down later?
faqs.answer: Take it down or update it. A case study is a claim with a date, not a hostage. Say that when you ask for the yes. Studios that refuse to edit a public page after a rebrand or a legal problem do not get the next approval.

markdown:
A case study approval process starts with a draft the client sees early, and with a written yes on what may be public. Agree the name, the numbers, and the screens before anyone falls in love with a layout. A case study that surprises the client does not get published. It gets a tense email, and then it gets pulled, which is a waste of the only story you were allowed to tell.

Treat the study as a joint document. You write it. They approve it. Nobody “just puts it live” because the design finally looks finished.

## What you are asking to show

Make a list, in plain language, at the start of the project or at the start of the write-up. Not at the end.

The name. Company, product, or a description with no name. Some clients can say “Thomas Bewick.” Some can only say “a heritage craft brand.” Decide which, and do not upgrade it in a caption later.

The work. A marketing site, an ecommerce migration, a product interface. Down the Cove can be described as an ecommerce migration and redesign because that is the public scope. Do not add a private metric because it would make the paragraph sound stronger.

The screens. Which URLs or frames may appear. A login wall, a customer record, or an unreleased product is a different conversation from the homepage. Default to no on anything a stranger should not see, including realistic data that looks like a real customer.

The numbers. Revenue, conversion, time saved, headcount. If you do not have permission and a real source, you do not have a number. Zero invented statistics. A study without a chart can still be specific: the constraint, the decision, the thing that shipped.

The quotes. Only a sentence the client has said and has approved in writing. Do not polish a quote into something they would not say out loud. If they will not be quoted, write the study without a quote. Attribution is not a decoration.

Google’s guide to [helpful, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for trustworthy pages with real experience behind them. A case study is that kind of page. First-hand work is the asset. A borrowed number is how a careful page becomes a liability the client has to disown.

## Show the draft while it is still easy to change

Send the outline before you send a designed page. The outline is a headline, five or six sentences, and the list of screens. Ask only: is this true, and are we allowed to say it. You will get a faster yes here than on a polished layout, because changing a sentence is cheap and changing a typeset page feels like a rejection.

Then send the written draft, still not the final art. Give them a date to reply, inside the window you can still use. “Comments by Friday. Silence means we hold, we do not assume yes.” Assuming yes is how surprises happen. A hold is annoying. A published surprise is worse.

Walk through the draft on a call if the stakes are high, and send the same draft in writing afterward. The writing is the record. The call is how you hear the flinch. If they flinch at a number, remove the number in the notes before you defend it. You can explain why you liked it. You cannot keep it.

One approver on their side. Legal, a founder, a marketing lead, whoever actually has the right. Feedback from a friend of the founder is not approval. Ask who signs, and send it to that person.

## A structure they can recognize

Use a structure that does not depend on hype. The reader, including the client, should find the same bones you already use for the work.

The constraint. What was true at the start. A shop that had to move without breaking the catalog. A heritage brand that needed a modern site. A product that had to be understandable on a small team. One constraint, not a origin myth.

The decision. What you refused, and what you made instead. Fewer templates. A type system instead of a new illustration for every section. A product screen with one primary action. The decision should be something the client remembers agreeing to. If they do not remember it, you are about to teach them their own project in public, which they will not enjoy.

What shipped. The pages or the interface, named accurately. Link to the live site if it is public. If it is not live, do not imply it is. Screenshots should match the build you are allowed to show, not an earlier concept you prefer.

What you will not claim. A short line is enough. “We are not publishing performance numbers.” That line protects both of you when a later editor wants to “add a stat.”

Keep the studio’s voice. Short sentences. No fake urgency. The client should recognize their project, not a campaign about your bravery. If a sentence embarrasses them, it does not belong, even if it is flattering to you.

## Screens, credits, and the small print

Crop screenshots so they do not reveal customer data, tokens, or unfinished admin tools. Blur is acceptable when the screen is otherwise the right screen. A blur over the entire point of the image means you picked the wrong image.

Name the tools only if they are true and useful. A Hanabi build might be Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, on Vercel, with Prisma and PostgreSQL when there is a real data layer. Do not add a stack you did not use because it sounds current. Credits for photographers, writers, and their team belong in the study if they did the work. A case study that implies the studio did the client’s decades of craft is a good way to lose the approval you just earned.

Logos and wordmarks need the same yes as the name. Some brands have rules about clear space and color. Follow them. A stretched logo in a case study is a strange way to demonstrate care.

If the study will be quoted by a search engine or an answer engine, the sentences still have to be true when lifted alone. The Princeton GEO paper, [Generative Engine Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735), treats quotations and citations as material those systems use. That is a reason to approve every quotable line, not a reason to stuff the page with slogans. A line that can be lifted should be a line the client would still sign.

## The yes, in writing

Ask for an explicit reply. “Approved to publish with the name, the screens attached, and no performance numbers.” Save it. If they approve with conditions, those conditions go into the draft before it ships, and you reply with the changed version for a final look if the change was meaningful.

Set a withdrawal path. If they need the study taken down later because a rebrand or a legal issue landed, you will do it. Say so. Studios that treat a case study as permanent hostage material do not get the next yes. A living page can be updated or retired. The approval was for a claim, and claims can expire.

Do not expand the study after approval. A new metric, a new screen, a new quote, each needs its own yes. “While we were in there” is how the approved draft becomes a different document. Small typographic fixes are fine. New facts are not.

If approval stalls, publish something else. A studio note that does not name them, about the method, may be fine if the agreement allows it. Do not publish the disguised version that is obviously them. They will notice. So will their customers.

## Where it lives

On your site, the study should match the live work. If the work has changed, update the screens or mark the study as a point in time. A page that shows last year’s product as if it were today’s is a new factual problem, not a nostalgia feature.

Send the client the link when it is up. They should not find it from a friend. Invite a correction window of a few days for factual misses, and say that taste comments after approval will be a new conversation. Then leave it alone.

If they ask for a change in that window, change the fact and reply with the new line so they can see it. Do not reopen the structure. A case study that is renegotiated every time someone forwards it will never stay true, because each reader will want a different emphasis. The approval you saved is what you point to. Offer a follow-up study later if the work itself has changed, rather than quietly stretching this one.

The next thing a future client will ask for, before they ever see that study, is often a short list of references. [References to send before a first call](/blog/references-to-send-before-a-first-call) is the piece to read next. Three links and one sentence each will do more than a folder, and it respects the same habit: show the specific thing, and say why it is there.

If you want to see studies’ worth of work in public, start from [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) only after you know which of your own references you are willing to stand behind. The call is more useful when both sides bring something specific.
